newsitem.title: INDIA: India's reformist Rao leaves legacy tainted.
newsitem.headline: India's reformist Rao leaves legacy tainted.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, who quit his last post in the Congress party on Thursday, won international praise for five years of reform that opened up the economy after decades of socialist control.
But in six months he went from the heights of political power to the humiliation of facing three criminal charges in separate court cases involving alleged vote-buying, cheating and forgery.
The charges forced Rao to resign last September as president of the Congress party, which has ruled India for all but five years since independence in 1947.
Rao, a former foreign, home and human resources minister, has denied any wrongdoing.
His resignation on Thursday, from his last remaining post as Congress chief in parliament, came after deputies pressured him to step down in the interests of party unity.
In April and May 1996, voters responded to his stewardship by dealing Congress a humiliating electoral defeat.
Although Congress suffered its worst defeat, Rao, 75, remained an influential voice by offering his party's crucial support to the centre-left United Front coalition government.
His hold over Congress came to an abrupt end after a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear as co-accused in a criminal conspiracy case.
The case stems from allegations by a businessman who says he was cheated of $100,000 which he had paid to a Hindu guru known to Rao to win a state contract in 1983. Rao has denied the allegation.
With Congress reeling from a string of other scandals, Rao's legal tangles appeared sure to tarnish his legacy.

Rao also faced court charges of buying votes in a narrowly won confidence motion in 1993 and of helping a forgery, involving an alleged attempt in 1989 to defame V.P. Singh, an opposition leader who later became prime minister.
The charges carry jail terms of between five and seven years.

Plucked from semi-retirement in 1991 to take over from the assassinated Rajiv Gandhi, Pamulaparthi Venkata Narasimha Rao's tact and patience made him the only person outside the Nehru- Gandhi family to complete a full term as prime minister.

His reticent, indecisive style irritated rivals and baffled supporters. "When I don't take a decision, it's not that I don't think about it," Rao said once. "I think about it and take a decision not to take a decision."

When Gandhi was murdered Rao, at the age of 69, was seen as the man who could rise above power struggles to unite the party. His lacklustre style did help cool social tensions of the times, which included caste conflicts and Hindu-Moslem riots.
During his term, Rao quelled a Maoist insurgency in the border state of Assam and successfully oversaw state polls in Punjab, where Sikh militants had battled for independence.
In the last two years of his tenure, India achieved economic growth of more than six percent a year. Trade more than doubled during Rao's term and inflation was reduced sharply.

During his rule, however, a separatist revolt in Kashmir peaked and fresh violence sprang up in September 1996 before the first elections in seven years were held in the state. Corruption allegations mounted during his tenure.

Rao was heavily criticised for his failure to take decisive action to prevent the 1992 destruction of a mosque by Hindu fanatics at Ayodhya or the nationwide riots which followed, in which some 3,000 people, mostly Moslems, died.
Rao, a widower since 1970, has undergone major heart surgery.
